bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Waste Emissions Charge for Petroleum and Natural Gas Systems: Procedures for Facilitating Compliance, Including Netting and Exemptions".
bill.latestActionText: Indefinitely postponed by Senate by Unanimous Consent.
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution nullifies the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rule titled Waste Emissions Charge for Petroleum and Natural Gas Systems: Procedures for Facilitating Compliance, Including Netting and Exemptions and published on November 18, 2024. The rule outlines compliance requirements under the Methane Emissions Reduction Program. Under the program, the EPA collects an annual charge on emissions of methane and other greenhouse gases from entities in the oil and gas sector if their emissions exceed specified waste emissions thresholds.

classification.plainSummary: This joint resolution would nullify an Environmental Protection Agency rule published in November 2024. That rule established procedures for charging oil and gas companies an annual fee when their methane and other greenhouse gas emissions exceed certain thresholds. If enacted, the resolution would eliminate these compliance requirements and the associated emissions charge program.

industries.rationale: The bill would eliminate a fee charged to oil and gas companies for methane emissions above specified thresholds.
Some electric utilities operate natural gas systems that could be subject to the emissions charge this resolution would nullify.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would cancel the EPA rule titled Waste Emissions Charge for Petroleum and Natural Gas Systems: Procedures for Facilitating Compliance, Including Netting and Exemptions and published on November 18, 2024.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys fuel or heats a home. People living near a road, a plant or a port.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in what fuel costs. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
